articles.title: Sustainability of violence prevention after a randomized vacant lot greening intervention in Philadelphia: A 10-y follow-up
articles.authors: Nicole Asa, Hiwot Y. Zewdie, Shadi Omidvar Tehrani, Maggie Beverly, Amy Carroll-Scott, Ali Rowhani-Rahbar, Andrew G. Rundle, Michelle C. Kondo, Jane E. Clougherty, Jessica Godwin, Charles C. Branas, Stephen J. Mooney
articles.abstract: Vacant lot greening has been shown to reduce violence and crime in the short-term [C. C. Branas et al. , Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 115 , 2946–2951 (2018)]. We assessed the 10-y impact of a 2013 clustered randomized controlled trial (RCT) of lot greening in Philadelphia on violence and crime. We measured lot greening by treatment assignment from the original 2013 cluster RCT and a longitudinal greening score to assess the sustainability of the treatment assignment from 2012 through 2023. Our outcomes were the annual reported total crime, violent crime, and firearm violent crime per square mile at each lot. We conducted intent-to-treat and contamination-adjusted intent-to-treat analyses to estimate the local average treatment effect on relative change in crime. Lots randomized to the full greening intervention remained greener over time compared to other lots. In intent-to-treat analyses, compared to lots that received no intervention, lots that received any intervention had a 9% decrease in density of any crime (estimate = 0.91, 95%CI = 0.86, 0.96) and a 9% decrease in violent crime (estimate = 0.91, 95%CI = 0.86, 0.97) per square mile per year. In contamination-adjusted analyses, compared to lots without sustained greening treatment, lots with sustained greening treatment had a 12% decrease in density of any crime (estimate = 0.88, 95%CI = 0.83, 0.93) and an 11% decrease in density of violent crime (estimate = 0.89, 95%CI = 0.83, 0.95) per square mile per year. Even after a decade, vacant lot greening continues to prevent violence.

articles.title: The debt burden of tropical cyclones and climate change
articles.authors: June Choi, Renzhi Jing, Christopher W. Callahan, Marshall Burke, Noah S. Diffenbaugh
articles.abstract: Addressing climate change through mitigation and adaptation is expected to require more than $6 trillion in global investment annually by 2035. Yet many countries face significant barriers to accessing this finance, including low or absent credit ratings, large debt burdens, and high borrowing costs. Climate change may further amplify these barriers, creating a “vicious cycle” in which mounting economic losses reduce the capacity of countries to invest in adaptation and mitigation. We provide evidence that the cost and availability of capital for many countries have already been shaped by both historical exposure to naturally-occurring tropical cyclones (TCs) and anthropogenic warming. Our empirical estimates suggest that, on average across TC-exposed countries, 20% of debt-to-GDP ratios are attributable to TCs from 1980 to 2019. Across all countries, GDP levels are on average 12% lower due to the combined impacts of baseline naturally-occurring TCs and anthropogenic warming. In a separate correlational machine-learning analysis, we estimate that these macroeconomic impacts are associated with an increased likelihood of hotter countries receiving credit ratings below investment grade ( < BBB–), as well as persistent credit risk premiums of at least 1 basis point in 64 countries and 5 basis points in highly exposed countries. We provide estimates for 181 countries, including many TC-affected and/or hot countries that do not have bond yield data. Future increases in temperature and TC activity may further worsen sovereign credit conditions, potentially undermining climate resilience and long-run development prospects.

articles.title: Stature reveals changing patterns of the biological standard of living in Europe and Asia over the past 7,000 y
articles.authors: Joerg Baten, Manon Stephan, Qiang Wang, Elizabeth Berger, John Brooke, Zhiwu Chen, Erdene Myagmar, Siân Halcrow, Kan Hou, Mark Hudson, Clark Spencer Larsen, Brian Padgett, Lanka Ranaweera, Charlotte Roberts, Noriko Seguchi, Richard H. Steckel, Xiaofan Sun, Naruphol Wangthongchaicharoen, Wanda Wang, Eun Jin Woo, Quanchao Zhang, Qun Zhang, Claudia Zancan, Qian Wang
articles.abstract: Human stature is a valuable indicator of nutritional status and health. Reconstructing this indicator allows insights into which types of societies were providing better health and nutrition—also termed the “biological standard of living” in the literature. Yet, archaeological evidence has not previously been assembled on a scale large enough for systematic comparison across premodern Eurasia. We present a dataset of 18,457 stature observations based on 783 sites from Asia and Europe, roughly spanning the 7,000 y before the twentieth century. Using harmonized estimates derived from long bones, we document broad regional variation in stature over time and examine how these patterns relate to population density and historical indicators of technological development. We observe marked declines in stature in most regions during the 500–1900 CE period, in both Asia and Europe. To interpret these patterns, we combine our stature series with estimates of population density, technological advancement, and related controls. As [Q. Ashraf, O. Galor, Am. Econ. Rev. 101 , 2003–2041 (2011)] predicted, higher technology levels were associated with higher population density, but not correlated with higher stature before the modern era. This relationship also holds after controlling for other potentially confounding factors such as latitude or transport access. By assembling the largest archaeological stature dataset for Eurasia to date and linking it to long-term demographic and historical indicators, this study provides an empirical basis for comparative research on premodern health, nutrition, and population pressure.

articles.title: Automating inequality? Gender bias in AI-mediated labor markets
articles.authors: Kenza Elass, Germain Gauthier, Debora Nozza, Paola Profeta
articles.abstract: Generative AI is rapidly entering labor markets, with large language models (LLMs) now used to help write CVs and evaluate applicants. We study the risks this creates in a series of audit experiments in which applicant gender is randomly assigned while all other information is held constant. We find that LLMs generate gender-stereotypical CVs and exhibit gender bias in screening scores and wage recommendations. Screening scores track occupational gender segregation, penalizing women in male-dominated occupations and favoring them in female-dominated ones. Wage recommendations track occupational gender wage gaps when gender is explicit in the prompt, though this gradient weakens under name-based gender signaling and is sensitive to the LLMs being used. These disparities arise through two channels: evaluation bias, when identical CV content is evaluated differently by gender, and generation bias, when gendered content produced by the model affects later evaluation. Because the same systems shape both CV content and its subsequent assessment, these channels can reinforce one another. Taken together, our findings identify measurable risks of algorithmic amplification in AI-mediated job search.

articles.title: Morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment
articles.abstract: Modern western legal and criminal justice theories assume that punishment should deter criminalized behavior by introducing costs that reduce its expected utility, but, empirically, punishment often has weak effects on rates of crime and recidivism. Here, we hypothesize that when people are motivated to engage in criminalized behavior for moral reasons, they show diminished sensitivity to punishment. We demonstrate our hypothesis across 10 correlational, experimental, and economic game studies with participants drawn from the general population as well as participants with criminal backgrounds. Studies 1 to 3 draw on federal data of over 30,000 offenders and find that participants’ estimates of moral motives for crime predict higher recidivism while estimates of material motives predict the opposite. Studies 4 to 8 use judgment studies and find that morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment across a diversity of crime types, when motives are manipulated but actions are kept constant, persist for different types of consequences, and are unique to moral motivation. Studies 9 and 10 employ economic games and find that when players take money from others for moral reasons, they are less deterred by the imposition of fines. Implications for systems of punishment, offender psychology, and restorative justice approaches are discussed.

articles.title: Coupled human–cattle mobility shaped the socioeconomic landscapes of the Holocene Middle Nile Valley
articles.authors: Marta Osypińska, Piotr Osypiński, Zdzislaw Belka, Louis Chaix, Patricia Anne Chiquet, Lionel Gourichon, Friederike Jesse, Olivier Langlois, Carlos Magnavita, Sonja Magnavita, Nadja Pöllath
articles.abstract: We present a synthesis of strontium isotope data ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr) from human and cattle dental enamel across Middle Nile. This dataset, which combines newly acquired and published measurements, reveals a complex history of human and cattle mobility linked to ecological gradients and sociocultural changes in this part of the continent. During the early Holocene (8,000 to 4,000 BCE), isotopic unanimity in human and cattle remains supports early, correlated mobility of humans and Bos , extending beyond Nile floodplains to adjacent uplands. In the mid-Holocene (4,000 to 1,000 BCE), isotopic data from Wadi Howar suggest bidirectional corridors for mobility of both species linking the Middle Nile and the Western Desert. This pattern correlates with the emergence of the Middle Nile civilizations in which cattle played a central cultural and economic role. From the first millennium BCE onward, a radical change can be observed, correlated with the progressive desertification processes in the Sahel. Although cattle import routes continued to follow wadi systems, they shifted south of the now desiccated Saharan lakes toward Kordofan. The long-term perspective emphasizes the continuous adaptation of societies in the Middle Nile of what is now Sudan and adjacent regions to environmental changes, aimed at maintaining sustained access to cattle, a resource that remained crucial for Middle Nile communities throughout the Holocene.

articles.title: Short-term flexibility and long-term stability in models of mind perception
articles.abstract: Understanding how people decide whether someone or something possesses a mind is central to a myriad of psychological, biological, and philosophical questions. It shapes fundamental processes at the individual (e.g., social interaction) and societal level (e.g., morality and ethics). While mind perception has been studied, it remains unclear which internal model people use when ascribing mental capacities to entities. Across four experiments (total N = 256), we explored what model people hold and its flexibility when ascribing agency and experience to entities encountered in everyday life and which differ in animacy and socialness (e.g., humans, pets, robots, voice assistants, tools). Using representational similarity analysis combined with lab-based experiments, a 6-wk long social interaction intervention, and longitudinal real-life exposure, we tested which model people use to ascribe agency and experience by comparing observed rating data to theoretical models. We demonstrated that an animacy distinction underlies the representational structure of experience attributions, while internal models for agency attributions are more idiosyncratic and flexible. When receiving explicit information on one entity, the internal model of agency changes. People update their model by incorporating this information, generalizing across the entire category of entities. We found no evidence that extended exposure to or ownership of inanimate technology, such as robots or voice assistants, or pets leads to restructuring of the models for experience or agency. Overall, these results provide insight into the internal models people hold when perceiving minds, the flexibility thereof, and offer ways to understand the roots and consequences of mind perception.

articles.title: No evidence for a universal effect of writing on language use or the evolution of syntax
articles.authors: Carlo Y. Meloni, Jessica K. Ivani, Taras Zakharko, Guanghao You, Kellen Parker van Dam, Chundra A. Cathcart, Balthasar Bickel
articles.abstract: The acquisition of writing has a lasting effect on how languages are processed in the brain, raising the possibility that it also affects how they are used and evolve over time. A popular hypothesis is that writing specifically leads to the increased use and evolution of complex hierarchical structures in language. While most case studies on individual languages have supported this, it remains unclear whether results scale to larger and more diverse sets of languages. Here we test this prediction in two ways: 1) synchronically, by modeling the effect of modality (written vs. nonwritten) on syntactic complexity, operationalized via hierarchy depth and clause count inside sentences, in corpora from 30 languages; and 2) diachronically, by modeling whether the development of writing affected the phylogenetic dynamics of hierarchy in clause combinations across 59 languages from three families. We found no effect of writing on the response variables in either analysis. Hierarchy depth and clause count inside sentences do not demonstrably differ between spoken and written use of language, and the introduction of writing had no discernible effect on the evolution of clause combinations in grammar. There is weak evidence for a decrease in variance in structural asymmetry after the introduction of writing in one family, possibly reflecting the impact of increased normativity. Our findings challenge popular beliefs about the relationship between writing and hierarchy and suggest that the evolution of syntax is more driven by culturally variable ideas about style in linguistic expression than by the evolution of writing.

articles.title: The sound of persuasion: Using generative AI to identify gender gaps in political influence
articles.authors: Ethan C. Busby, Lisa P. Argyle, Parker Davis, Joshua R. Gubler, Bryce Hepner, Christopher F. Karpowitz, Alex Lyman, Justin Olcott, Jessica R. Preece, David Wingate
articles.abstract: Women often experience a deficit in persuasive influence, particularly in contexts like politics, where expectations about women’s behavior may conflict with gendered expectations about the domain and role. In spite of this widespread pattern, the mechanisms behind the gender gap in persuasion are difficult to isolate and test in dynamic political conversations. Women may be less persuasive simply because role-based expectations prompt others to afford women less authority when speaking about politics generally or about some political topics. Alternatively, women may be less persuasive because they tend to use linguistic patterns or rhetorical strategies that are less effective. Using an original AI-based approach, we put 4,300 human subjects into realistic, real-time phone conversations with an AI agent. These agents were randomly assigned either a masculine or feminine gendered conversation topic and a male- or female-sounding voice, allowing us to manipulate topic and perceptions of speakers’ gender while holding constant other elements of rhetorical content and strategy. After validating the experimental treatments, we find no direct effects of perceived gender of the AI agent, as cued by voice. However, gender affects other important aspects of the persuasive interaction. Research subjects were more likely to be persuaded about the masculine topic (defense spending) than the feminine topic (aid to the poor). Additionally, women research subjects were, on average, more persuaded than men. To the extent that men and women emphasize different topics in political conversations and have different discussion partners, these dynamics are likely to shape women’s political persuasive influence.

articles.title: Behind stable richness, more European pollinators are losing than gaining
Impact pathways of a jurisdictional approach to slowing deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon
articles.authors: Jill L. Caviglia-Harris, Thales A. P. West, Daniel W. Harris, Erin O. Sills, Katrina Mullan
articles.abstract: Governance of many of the world’s largest remaining tropical forests is shared across multiple levels of government, giving subnational jurisdictions a central role in forest management. This has motivated growing interest in jurisdictional approaches (JAs) to control deforestation. For JAs to deliver on national and international conservation priorities, those priorities must be translated into incentives that reduce deforestation at the jurisdictional level. Brazil’s Priority List (PL), launched in 2008, creates such incentives by identifying high-deforestation municipalities, subjecting them to intensified monitoring, enforcement, and credit restrictions, and establishing jurisdiction-wide criteria for exit that make municipalities accountable for deforestation within their borders. While prior studies show that the PL reduces deforestation, it remains unclear where these reductions occur and whether there is displacement across land tenure types or into neighboring municipalities. We assemble a municipality-level panel dataset for the Brazilian Legal Amazon (2000–2024) that combines PL designations with annual deforestation disaggregated by land tenure. Using a heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences estimator, we estimate effects within and across municipalities. We find large and statistically significant reductions concentrated on private lands, including agrarian reform settlements and other private properties. Within listed municipalities, we find no evidence of decreased or increased clearing in Protected Areas, Indigenous Territories, or undesignated public lands. Total deforestation also declines in neighboring municipalities, with reductions concentrated on private lands. These findings are consistent with the PL translating national conservation priorities into local land-use change while limiting displacement, offering insights for the design of jurisdictional approaches aimed at forest conservation.

articles.title: Music illuminates sociocultural dimensions of autobiographical memory
articles.authors: Cara Turnbull, Benjamin M. Kubit, Kelly Jakubowski, Elizabeth H. Margulis
articles.abstract: Researchers have long theorized that autobiographical memory relies on sociocultural structures, such as life scripts and event schemas. The potency of music as a marker of social and personal identity, combined with its ubiquity in everyday life, allows us to connect these everyday scripts to larger patterns of socially and culturally shaped behavior. We collected free-response descriptions of autobiographical memories evoked by short clips of familiar songs from university undergraduates (n = 233). The songs spanned three popular genres and aligned with two significant periods of listeners’ lives. We analyzed the similarities and differences in the content of memories for particular songs using natural language processing. Memories cued by songs from the same category displayed striking similarities, suggesting that particular types of music cue memories that are similar between listeners but that vary according to characteristics such as music genre and release date. Two control conditions, in which a new set of participants reported memories evoked by key words from the lyrics (n = 121) and short narrative summaries of the lyrics (n = 129), indicate that these results cannot be explained by within-category similarities in the songs’ lyrical content. Instead, we suggest that the intersubjective structure of music-evoked autobiographical memories reflects socioculturally-defined scripts tied to song characteristics such as genre and release date. Thus, while memories may feel idiosyncratic and personal, there are also substantial similarities in life experiences between individuals with broadly similar backgrounds, and these shared experiences can be spontaneously called to mind through the seemingly innocuous act of turning on the radio.

articles_hidden.title: Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 participates in the internalization of arginine-rich dipeptide repeat proteins
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandra B. Sutter, Benito F. Buksh, Jelena Mojsilovic-Petrovic, Casey Dalton, Nicholas A. Till, Danielle C. Morgan, Gopinath Krishnan, Evan Kaspi, David W. C. MacMillan, Robert G. Kalb
articles_hidden.abstract: Microsatellite repeat expansion of the 5′ GGGGCC 3′ sequence in the C9orf72 gene is the most common monogenic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia. Dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) translated from the mutant allele can be detected in postmortem brains of afflicted individuals. The arginine containing peptides, poly proline-arginine (poly-PR) and poly glycine-arginine (poly-GR), are particularly noxious to cells. Both can undergo cell-to-cell transmission, but underlying mechanisms are not understood. We found rapid internalization and nucleolar localization of bath-applied hemagglutinin (HA) tagged poly-PR with twenty repeats (HA-PR 20 ) in cell lines and neurons. Small molecule and RNAi approaches implicated a temperature-dependent, fluid phase endocytosis mechanism for HA-PR 20 . We sought to identify DPR-related cell surface uptake factors using µMap high-resolution proximity labeling. DPR–iridium conjugates identified candidate cell-surface proteins which were interrogated in a secondary RNAi screen. Focusing on our strongest candidate, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 (CSPG4), we showed cellular uptake of HA-PR 20 is reduced by inhibition of glycosaminoglycan chain synthesis and knockdown or ablation of CSPG4. Knockdown of CSPG4 protected PR 20 -induced neuronal toxicity. Using a dual reporter system to interrogate in vitro neuron-to-neuron transmission of PR 50, we found PR 50 synthesized by one neuron readily spread to neighboring cells. Transmission was significantly reduced with CSPG4 knockdown. Similarly conditioned media from PR 50 or GR 50 expressing neurons contained transmissible protein that was internalized into neurons in a CSPG4-dependent manner. These results suggest CSPG4 participates in poly-PR/poly-GR internalization and transmission.

articles_hidden.title: Counterions, polarization, and pore hydration relay drive ion permeation through hydrophobic pore formed by the MERS coronavirus E protein
articles_hidden.authors: Zhongyi Wan, Mei Hong, Qiang Cui
articles_hidden.abstract: Hydrophobic pores are generally expected to exclude ions because the large desolvation penalty associated with ion transfer cannot be compensated within a nonpolar environment. The envelope (E) protein of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) presents a striking exception, conducting cations with high efficiency despite forming a predominantly hydrophobic pore. To resolve this apparent paradox, we combine finite-temperature string simulations with additive and polarizable force fields to determine the minimum free-energy pathways for ion permeation through the MERS E channel. The simulations reveal a cooperative permeation mechanism in which transient counterion association, localized pore hydration, and electronic polarization jointly reduce the desolvation penalty. Rather than acting as passive spectators, counterions transiently chaperone the permeating cation before dissociating within the channel, thereby lowering the energetic cost of charge desolvation while preserving net ionic conductance. Explicit electronic polarization further reshapes the pore hydration landscape and cation– π interactions, leading to substantially reduced free-energy barriers and a permeation mechanism that is in substantially better agreement with experiment. These results suggest that efficient ion transport through hydrophobic pores arises from the cooperative interplay between electrostatics, polarization, and hydration rather than complete pore wetting, providing both a mechanistic framework for MERS E protein function and a general physical principle for ion transport through biological and synthetic hydrophobic nanopores.

articles_hidden.title: Resilient j = 3/2 superconductivity in topological semimetal YPtBi
articles_hidden.authors: Prathum Saraf, Nicholas A. Crombie, Rahul Sharma, Jared Z. Dans, Danila Sokratov, Carsyn L. Mueller, Ram Kumar, Hyunsoo Kim, Connor Roncaioli, Winslow Weiss, Arthur Carlton-Jones, Peter Y. Zavalij, David Graf, Chandra Shekhar, Steven M. Anlage, Claudia Felser, Johnpierre Paglione
articles_hidden.abstract: Cooper pairing in most of the known fermionic superfluids occurs via spin-1/2 quasiparticle interactions that lead to spin-singlet or spin-triplet pairing. In the topological semimetal YPtBi, strong spin–orbit coupling results in a band inversion between highly symmetric s - and p -like electronic bands and a degeneracy at the Γ point that ensures the manifold of j = 3/2 quasiparticle states thrive near the Fermi level, where superconducting pairing occurs. Here we study the effects of magnetic and nonmagnetic disorder and carrier density on this exotic superconducting pairing state. By varying levels of disorder and carrier densities by nearly two and three orders of magnitude, respectively, we show that the superconducting critical temperature of YPtBi has a remarkable robustness, with little variation across this span. Our results suggest that superconductivity in YPtBi may reside in a regime where phase stiffness, rather than pair formation, governs the transition temperature. The insensitivity of Cooper pairing to dramatic changes in quasiparticle environment in a j = 3/2 superconductor highlights a form of protection realized in topological high-spin superconductors.

articles_hidden.title: Neuronal IL-34 programs microglial activity via the TGF-β–MEF2C axis to constrain neuroinflammation following brain ischemia
articles_hidden.authors: Minshu Li, Xu Zhou, Ran Li, Hanchen Liu, Caiyun Qi, Wenjun Zhang, Yali Han, Tingyu Yin, Sarah Wu, Yan Pan, Decai Tian, Tao Yan, Jie Zhou, Xiaochun Chen, Qiang Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Brain ischemia induces robust neuroinflammation driven by microglial activation, yet whether ischemic neurons actively reprogram microglial phenotypes to limit inflammation remains elusive. Here, we identify neuronal interleukin-34 (IL-34) as a critical immunomodulatory signal that maintains microglial homeostasis after cerebral ischemia. We demonstrate that ischemic injury augments IL-34-CSF1R signaling between neurons and microglia. Neuron-specific overexpression of Il34 (Syn1- Il34 tg mice) attenuated infarct volume and neurodeficits after middle cerebral artery occlusion, whereas neuronal Il34 knockdown exacerbated brain injury. Microglial depletion abolished IL-34-mediated neuroprotection, suggesting microglia as essential effectors. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that neuronal IL-34 preserved homeostatic microglial signatures ( P2ry12, Cx3cr1, Tgfbr1 ), while suppressing inflammatory activities ( Il1b, Tnf, Cxcl2 ) through upregulation of the transcription factor MEF2C. Mechanistically, IL-34 activated TGF-β signaling in microglia and inhibition of TGF-β signaling abolished the protective effects of IL-34, whereas microglia-specific Mef2c overexpression rescued neuroprotection despite TGF-β blockade. Thus, ischemic neurons deploy IL-34 to orchestrate the immunoregulatory activity of microglia via the TGF-β–MEF2C axis, representing a previously unrecognized endogenous mechanism counteracting neuroinflammation. Our study reveals neuronal IL-34 as a potential therapeutic target for ischemic stroke.

articles_hidden.title: Transoceanic dispersals and island extinctions shape global snipe and woodcock diversity
articles_hidden.authors: Min Zhao, João Marcos Guimarães Capurucho, Brian J. Stucky, David W. Steadman, John M. Bates, Michelle J. LeFebvre, Robert P. Guralnick, Julie M. Allen, Jessica A. Oswald
articles_hidden.abstract: Island colonization through transoceanic dispersal has been central in shaping insular biodiversity. Following colonization, island populations often undergo morphological shifts, which may promote ecological specialization and endemism, but often increase vulnerability to extinction. Most species in the shorebird family Scolopacidae are highly migratory, which likely underpins their propensity for long-distance dispersal. Notably, snipes ( Gallinago , Coenocorypha ) and woodcocks ( Scolopax ) have colonized diverse island regions, including the southwest Pacific, Malay Archipelago, Japan’s Amami, and the Caribbean, although none of the extant island endemics are migratory. The southwest Pacific and Caribbean taxa have suffered substantial recent extinction driven by human impacts. Here, we investigate avian evolutionary and biogeographic dynamics using a combination of morphology and phylogenomic data from target capture sequencing of key extant and extinct snipes and woodcocks. Our results reveal four independent dispersals from the Eastern to Western Hemisphere and a trans-Pacific dispersal from South America to the southwest Pacific islands. Comparative analyses of migratory behavior and morphology demonstrate pronounced changes in insular groups. For example, the small Austral snipes Coenocorypha are nested within Gallinago , sister to a group of much larger, continental South American snipes. Another case is the extinct Scolopax brachycarpa of Hispaniola which osteologically more resembles Scolopax , but genetically belongs to Gallinago . Gallinago brachycarpa and other extinct Caribbean snipes may represent a radiation that is lost forever. Our findings shed light on the processes that generate and erase avian diversity on islands, highlighting the dynamic interplay of dispersal, adaptation to novel conditions, and risk for extinction.

articles_hidden.title: Calculated residue protonation states find functional, conserved E-channel proton-loading sites in Complex I from bacteria to mammals
articles_hidden.authors: Md. Raihan Uddin, Koreena Sookhai, Junjun Mao, Gehan Ranepura, Cat Chenal, Rongmei Wei, Jose Ortiz-Soto, Hagar Ibrahim, Robert L. Burnap, M. R. Gunner
articles_hidden.abstract: Bioenergetic proton pumps take protons from one side of a membrane, transiently binding them at a loading site within the protein matrix, and then release them to the other side against an electrochemical gradient. The E channel of Complex I, from bacteria to mammals, contains a conserved proton-loading region whose function is distributed among several interacting residues. Noting extensive sequence divergence across homologous Complex I structures, we asked how this function is conserved during evolution despite many amino acid changes. Multi-Conformation Continuum Electrostatics (MCCE) calculations were performed on the five E-channel subunits from 41 experimental structures from bacteria, cyanobacteria, insects, and mammals. A Monte Carlo sampling identified five to seven residues in each species that function as a proton-loading cluster. Structures with a closed E-channel have ~1 more proton in the cluster than those with open conformations. Proton binding represents ensemble averages across thousands of accessible microstates, each with an integer protonation state. A mean-field analysis showed that the proton affinity depends on both titrating residues and the surrounding protein electrostatic environment. Closely related proteins use nearly the same cluster of residues, whereas more divergent proteins substitute alternative proton-handling residues and modify electrostatically important fixed-charge groups to preserve cluster proton affinity. Thus, E-channel reversible proton-loading is preserved during sequence evolution by maintaining a local “electrostatic architecture,” often involving quite different evolutionary solutions. Thus, conservation of E-channel proton loading depends more strongly on the local electrostatic environment than on conservation of the individual residues that create it.

articles_hidden.title: Molecular interactions underlying selective partitioning of clients into MED1 and FUS condensates
articles_hidden.authors: Ikki Yasuda, Eiji Yamamoto, Kenji Yasuoka, Kresten Lindorff-Larsen
articles_hidden.abstract: Biomolecular condensates selectively recruit and exclude proteins, and this partitioning is sometimes dictated by their intrinsically disordered regions. Factors that determine partitioning include client–scaffold interactions and stabilization of the scaffold network within the condensate, yet a molecular and predictive understanding has not been fully achieved. Here, we used coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate molecular interactions between two types of nuclear proteins as scaffolds: the charge-rich disordered region of Mediator 1 (MED1) and the aromatic-rich disordered region of Fused in Sarcoma (FUS), in mixtures with client intrinsically disordered regions from six different proteins. We show distinct partitioning into the MED1 and FUS condensates, while the presence of RNA in both dilute and dense phases modulated client partitioning. Favorable client–scaffold interaction energies within condensates were associated with client partitioning, while client–scaffold interactions competed with scaffold self-interactions. Analysis of interaction energies of individual residues revealed that the interactions were localized to specific sequence regions: charged blocks for interactions with MED1, and dispersed aromatic residues for interactions with FUS. Using residue–resolved interaction energies from our molecular dynamics simulations, we developed sequence-based predictors of client partitioning into MED1 and FUS condensates. Our prediction approach for partitioning can be extended to other biomolecules, offering a framework to analyze their partitioning in cellular environments.

articles_hidden.title: Diffusive and advective transport in structurally anisotropic fibrous hydrogels
articles_hidden.authors: Yuhang Huang, Junjie Yin, Xiao He, Arun Ramachandran, Hani E. Naguib, Eugenia Kumacheva
articles_hidden.abstract: Changes in fiber orientation in structurally anisotropic fibrous extracellular matrices govern transport, distribution, and accumulation of biologically active molecules and therapeutic nanoparticles in tissues. Fundamental studies of advection-driven transport in such matrices are challenging because changes in network anisotropy are generally coupled with variation in fiber dimensions, density, and surface chemistry. Here, a fibrous hydrogel was engineered in which the type and degree of fiber orientation were decoupled from these structural characteristics. Advection of charge-neutral nanoparticle probes under physiologically relevant pressure gradients was studied in a channel geometry that imposed spatially nonuniform flow across the fibrous network. The probe advection was quantified by the time of probe permeation through the gel along the fastest flow path and the time of probe distribution within the gel. We show that the permeation timescale was governed by advection along the pressure gradient, whereas the distribution timescale transitioned between advection- and diffusion-limited behavior depending on fiber orientation and probe dimension. The decoupling between these timescales became more pronounced with stronger alignment along the pressure gradient and with increasing probe dimension. Scaling analysis and a fluid dynamics simulation model further provided mechanistic insight into these experimental findings. Together, these results identify the key structural factors governing advection in anisotropic fibrous networks and provide a platform for future studies of the role of fiber orientation in tissues in regulating the transport, distribution, and dissemination of biologically active molecules, exosomes, and nanoparticle therapeutics under interstitial fluid flow.

articles_hidden.title: Paul R. Ehrlich: Visionary pioneer and public scientist for nature and humanity
articles_hidden.authors: Gretchen C. Daily, Rodolfo Dirzo, Carl Folke, John P. Holdren, Simon A. Levin
articles_hidden.abstract: Paul R. Ehrlich is legendary for his scientific insight and impact—and even more so for bringing science to the public through writing, speaking, and, most famously, twenty-some appearances on the Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson. He was quick-witted—he would readily add quick-tempered, with chagrin—and could bring down a house. Paul cherished deep friendships and nature. He loved collaborating with his wife of 71 years, Anne H. Ehrlich, and with innumerable students and colleagues all over the world. He made transformative contributions of astonishing range, including in ecology and evolution, biodiversity and conservation, human population and overconsumption, and the integration of ecology and economics. He was deeply committed to racial and social justice, reflected in his actions and writing.

articles_hidden.title: A periplasmic regulator establishes adaptive impermeability to control carbapenem entry
articles_hidden.authors: Verena Ducret, Catarina Gonçalves Milho, Diego Gonzalez, Karl Perron
articles_hidden.abstract: Outer-membrane permeability is a major determinant of antibiotic susceptibility in Gram-negative bacteria and is generally thought to be controlled through transcriptional regulation of porin expression. Here we identify the small periplasmic protein PtrA as a regulator of OprD-dependent carbapenem permeability in Pseudomonas aeruginosa . PtrA promotes imipenem resistance without altering OprD abundance, associates with OprD-containing membrane complexes and reduces intracellular imipenem entry. Using zinc and copper as complementary physiological signals, we show that PtrA-mediated permeability control is mechanistically distinct from CzcRS-dependent repression of oprD and precedes transcriptional porin depletion. These findings define a two-phase mechanism in which rapid periplasmic regulation provides an immediate adaptive response before transcriptional remodeling of the outer membrane. Our work identifies adaptive impermeability as a previously unrecognized mechanism linking environmental sensing to dynamic control of bacterial outer-membrane permeability.

articles_hidden.title: Preemptive solving of future problems: Multitask Preplay in humans and machines
articles_hidden.authors: Wilka Carvalho, Sam Hall-McMaster, Honglak Lee, Samuel J. Gershman
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans can pursue a near-infinite variety of tasks, but typically can only pursue a small number at the same time. We hypothesize that humans leverage experience on one task to preemptively learn solutions to other tasks that were accessible but not pursued. We formalize this idea as “Multitask Preplay”, an algorithm that replays experience on one task as the starting point for “preplay”—counterfactual simulation of an accessible but unpursued task. Preplay is used to learn a predictive representation that can support fast, adaptive task performance later on. When implemented within deep reinforcement learning, it predicts human generalization to novel tasks more accurately than traditional planning and predictive representation methods across grid-worlds and a 2D Minecraft domain. Additionally, Multitask Preplay improves an artificial agent’s ability to generalize to new environments sharing task co-occurrence structure. These findings demonstrate that Multitask Preplay is a scalable theory of human counterfactual learning and generalization; endowing artificial agents with this capacity can significantly improve their performance in challenging multitask environments.

articles_hidden.title: Surfing sequence landscapes with sequence–structure augmentation
articles_hidden.authors: Aidan T. Cosgrove, Charles L. Brooks

articles_hidden.title: An ensemble of functionally distinct factors enables spatial quality control during proteasome base assembly
articles_hidden.authors: Eshita Das, Linh Le, Richard Kim, James D. Orth, Soyeon Park
articles_hidden.abstract: The proteasome is an essential mediator of the ubiquitin–proteasome system and a complex molecular machine. Hallmarks of de novo proteasome assembly include dedicated chaperones and many subunits, culminating into major assembly intermediates such as the base. Emerging evidence suggests that proteasome assembly is subject to extensive quality control (QC). To understand mechanisms of QC, we examined a crucial assembly checkpoint during base assembly. Our findings reveal sequential mechanisms of QC, in which a checkpoint complex is first assembled, then sequestered into the nucleus, away from ongoing proteasome assembly in the cytoplasm. Assembly of this checkpoint complex depends on noncanonical ubiquitination of the Nas2 chaperone. The Nas2 ubiquitin chain functions as a scaffold by binding the Rpn13 ubiquitin receptor, which is distantly positioned within the same complex. Rpn13 also positions the ubiquitin chain to its neighboring Hul5 ubiquitin ligase, for continual chain elongation to further stabilize this complex. Ubiquitin-mediated assembly enables spatial sequestration of this checkpoint complex through its intrinsic nuclear localization signal (NLS). This NLS on Rpt4 specifically targets this checkpoint complex into the nucleus, emphasizing the importance of spatial compartmentalization. Our findings reveal that proteasome assembly integrates multiple functionally distinct components as QC factors (1 assembly chaperone, 2 ubiquitin regulators, and 1 NLS) to distinguish correct vs. incorrect assembly events en route to a proteasome holoenzyme. These components are not simply passengers in assembly intermediates with their activities reserved for mature proteasomes, but their fundamental functions in cellular proteolysis may begin by first ensuring the accuracy of proteasome assembly.

articles_hidden.title: The evolution and function of eukaryote-to-cyanobacteria horizontal gene transfer
articles_hidden.authors: Xuwen Cao, Chao Liu, Daixi Liu, Yanyan Wang, Jacob L. Steenwyk, Xin Zhong, Yafei Wang, Hongyue Liu, Qiang Zhang, Xing-Xing Shen, Zhishuai Qu, Changwei Shao, Shengying Li, Yuanning Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Prokaryote-to-eukaryote horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has emerged as a driver of eukaryotic evolution. In contrast, eukaryote-to-prokaryote HGT remains poorly characterized, limiting insight into how eukaryote-derived genes influence prokaryotic evolution and function. Here, we reconstructed a comprehensive and well-resolved phylogeny of 469 high-quality Cyanobacteria genomes spanning all orders. Leveraging this framework, we identified 204 candidate functionally diverse genes of eukaryotic origin in cyanobacteria, likely representing 59 putative transfer events, including 197 genes not previously documented. All 204 candidates were intronless, consistent with intron loss during their evolutionary history. Transcriptomics reveal that HGT-acquired genes are expressed at significantly higher levels than both genome-wide and functionally matched non-HGT-acquired genes, suggesting functional importance. Notably, 138 genes exhibited functional annotations absent from the host cyanobacteria. We further characterized a granule-bound starch synthase (GBSS) putatively acquired by Crocosphaera from an ancestral archaeplastid lineage, enabling starch synthesis that may facilitate energy storage for nocturnal nitrogen fixation. These findings reveal that eukaryote-to-prokaryote gene transfer is an underappreciated driver of cyanobacterial evolution and function, with broad implications for microbial ecology, functional adaptation, and cross-domain genetic exchange.

articles_hidden.title: Endosomal mRNA transport coordinates local mitochondrial bioenergetics during polar fungal growth
articles_hidden.authors: Johannes Postma, Pascal Künzel, Simon Wegmann, Kira Müntjes, Senthil-Kumar Devan, Srimeenakshi Sankaranarayanan, Stephan Krueger, Sebastian Hänsch, Philipp Westhoff, Stefanie Weidtkamp-Peters, Nick Wierckx, Lasse van Wijlick, Michael Feldbrügge
articles_hidden.abstract: Mitochondrial function relies on the precise spatial coordination of protein synthesis and import. Most mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded and must be supplied across varying intracellular distances. In highly polarized cells such as fungal hyphae and neurons, active long-distance mRNA transport is thought to sustain distal mitochondrial function, but its mechanistic coupling to protein import and organelle physiology is unclear. Here, we demonstrate that endosomal transport of mRNAs encoding mitochondrial proteins orchestrates local bioenergetics in infectious hyphae of Ustilago maydis . Using the subunit Atp3 of electron transport chain Complex V as a model, we uncover that the endosomal mRNA transporter Rrm4 is required for efficient mitochondrial protein import, particularly at growth poles. Loss of Rrm4 leads to defects in mitochondrial import, resulting in altered physiology. We propose that endosome-coupled mRNA transport constitutes a fundamental layer of subcellular mitochondrial homeostasis, with implications extending from fungal pathogenicity to neuronal disease.

articles_hidden.title: Evolution, information content, and optimality of gene regulatory architectures
articles_hidden.authors: Nicholas H. Barton, Gašper Tkačik
articles_hidden.abstract: Evolution of genetic regulatory sequences is shaped by their genotype–phenotype map, but this map itself can evolve via changes in the molecular machinery that reads out the regulatory sequences. Using population genetics theory, we derive a maximization principle, which implies that genotype–phenotype maps will evolve to associate fit phenotypes with larger numbers of possible genotypes. Mathematically, this builds on analogies between population genetics and statistical physics, as well as optimal coding in information theory. The results are particularly interesting in the context of transcriptional regulation, where optimal values of certain parameters that determine the gene regulatory architecture can be derived even without a complete knowledge of the molecular mechanisms involved. We illustrate the theory using a simplified model of transcription factor (TF) binding to cis-regulatory elements (CREs): the fraction of possible CREs across the entire genotype space that bind a given TF evolves to match the fraction of CREs under selection to bind that TF. Similar “frequency matching” results are expected to emerge generically, because selection implicitly moves the entire regulatory architecture toward a fitness maximum, determining the “replicated genotype–phenotype map” for all CREs, while it simultaneously adapts toward individually fit CREs on that map. We discuss the subtleties and limitations of the theory related to biophysical constraints and the need for mutational robustness. Last, our theory suggests a possible mathematical definition for evolvability with predictive power that can be tested in evolutionary simulations and, ultimately, in comparative genetics studies.

articles_hidden.title: Bouton-specific diversity of glutamate release from single parallel fiber axons in the cerebellum
articles_hidden.authors: Théo Rossi, Anthime Perrot, Aline Huber, Bernard Poulain, Frédéric Doussau, Antoine M. Valera, Philippe Isope
articles_hidden.abstract: Sensorimotor processing relies on high-frequency signaling across widespread neuronal networks, during which synapses undergo rapid short-term plasticity (STP) that transiently enhances or depresses synaptic strength. Although STP is known to vary across cell types and postsynaptic targets, it remains unclear whether and how it is regulated at the level of individual synaptic boutons along the same axon. Here, we used two-photon imaging of a fast genetically encoded glutamate sensor expressed in cerebellar granule cells to monitor glutamate release from individual parallel fiber boutons during trains of activity. We showed that along single axons, glutamate transients were detected at nearly all boutons, and displayed a high diversity of STP profiles. At individual boutons, initial synaptic weight and STP were regulated separately. Synaptic weight was primarily driven by release probability ( P r ) and the apparent number of functional release sites ( N ), whereas STP was mainly supported by rapid mobilization of synaptic vesicles. At the molecular level, we show that Synapsin II contributes to bouton-specific heterogeneity in release properties. These findings reveal that STP is regulated at the level of individual boutons by specific molecular determinants, enabling fine-tuned control of information flow in cerebellar circuits. A single granule cell could therefore translate an identical presynaptic spike pattern into distinct release dynamics at each of its boutons, thus diversifying the temporal structure of the information delivered to Purkinje cells.

articles_hidden.title: Visualization of actin filaments in Plasmodium falciparum blood cell stages
articles_hidden.authors: Andrés Guillén-Samander, Jana Dröge, Vendula Horáčková, Isabelle G. Henshall, Tobias Spielmann
articles_hidden.abstract: The actin cytoskeleton is crucial to regulate cellular processes and morphology in eukaryotes, yet the tools to visualize it are not compatible with all organisms. In the apicomplexan Plasmodium falciparum , actin filaments are thought to be short and unstable, complicating their visualization. Here, we show that a tandem fusion of the actin-chromobody can label filaments in all P. falciparum red blood cell stages and observe actin structures in live cells with high spatiotemporal resolution. This work suggests that previous lack of labeling was due to suboptimal probes and that malaria blood stages have a filamentous and highly dynamic actin network.

articles_hidden.title: isSPA-vesicle: AI-assisted structure determination of membrane proteins on vesicles
articles_hidden.authors: Mingjie Zhao, Duanfang Cao, Ziqi Cheng, Yuhan Hu, Yang He, Shaobo Wang, Xuepeng Wei, Xinzheng Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: The demand for three-dimensional reconstruction of membrane proteins in native lipid environments has grown substantially in recent years. Both single-particle analysis and tomographic techniques have enabled structural studies across diverse vesicular samples; however, these methods remain limited in either efficiency or resolution. Here, we present an AI-enabled, vesicle geometry-guided 3D reconstruction strategy based on untilted data. Given that some vesicles exhibit anisotropic shapes in solution and adopt near-spherical or ellipsoidal geometries, we trained an AI model to estimate membrane geometric parameters and compute normal vectors based on the fitted ellipsoidal surface. This information facilitates post hoc filtering of particles picked using the isSPA framework based on the angular difference between their orientations and the membrane normals, and also enables the exclusion of particles outside the vesicles. This allows efficient localization of target membrane proteins enabling near-atomic-resolution reconstruction. Using this approach, we efficiently reconstructed membrane proteins ranging from 130 kDa to 2 MDa across two classes of enveloped viruses and three types of synthetic liposomes, achieving 2.7 Å resolution for influenza A virus hemagglutinin and 3.1 Å for the prefusion spike protein of HCoV-OC43. Our method provides a simple and efficient tool for achieving such reconstructions in physiological lipid bilayers.

articles_hidden.title: Four phases and temporal threshold of population calcium response during locomotion in cortical astrocytes
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Fedotova, Alexey Brazhe, Alexey Semyanov
articles_hidden.abstract: Calcium activity is a major form of astrocyte excitability. Astrocytic calcium events arise spontaneously and in response to behavior, but how unitary events shape population-level activity remains unclear. Using two-photon imaging in the primary somatosensory cortex of awake mice running on a freely rotating disk, we analyzed calcium dynamics during quiescence and locomotion. During quiescence, population fluctuations were driven mainly by the co-occurrence of new events rather than by their enlargement. During locomotion, responses progressed through four phases: emergence of new events, their merging into a superevent, fragmentation, and an afterburst. These responses combined the progressive recruitment of active regions with amplification of a reproducible spatial calcium pattern. New events emerged within the first seconds after locomotion onset, indicating a rapid astrocytic response. A full population response required about 5 s of locomotion: Shorter episodes failed to develop the superevent and produced markedly smaller responses. In suprathreshold episodes, the superevent displayed a reproducible ΔF/F pattern. Hotspots within this pattern had shorter latencies and were also more active during quiescence. A dynamic mode decomposition with control model driven by synthetic or real locomotion inputs reproduced the response phases, temporal threshold, and superevent pattern. These findings show that locomotion-evoked astrocytic calcium activity is an ordered, threshold-dependent population process with reproducible spatiotemporal structure that can be approximated by a low-dimensional dynamical system.

articles_hidden.title: Causal dynamic resonance reduces false positives in detecting causality
articles_hidden.authors: Claudia Lainscsek, Pariya Salami, Simon Dräger, Adi R. Bulsara, Sydney S. Cash, Terrence J. Sejnowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Many dynamical systems in nature, such as brains and weather systems, are highly nonlinear and complex. Determining information flow among the components that make up these dynamical systems is challenging. If the components are the result of a common process or become synchronized, causality measures typically fail. We previously introduced Cross-Dynamical Delay Differential Analysis, a nonlinear method for assessing causal influence, along with a complementary approach for dynamical similarity between time series data, Dynamical Ergodicity Delay Differential Analysis. Here, we show that “Causal Dynamic Resonance (CDR)” further improves the false positive rejection rate by adding white noise to the data, without perturbing the underlying dynamical system. This is followed by a study of CDR in coupled Rössler systems, where ground truth interactions are known and in invasive intracranial electroencephalographic data from drug-resistant epilepsy patients undergoing presurgical monitoring.

articles_hidden.title: Physicochemical microenvironments within biomolecular condensates govern reaction kinetics beyond mass-action effects
articles_hidden.authors: Jangwon Bae, Kibeom Hong, Donghyuk Lee, Jaebum Jun, Yongwon Jung
articles_hidden.abstract: Cells utilize phase separation to compartmentalize biochemical reactions within biomolecular condensates. Although these compartments can enhance reaction rates by concentrating reactants, how they modulate kinetics beyond mass-action effects remains poorly understood. Here, using spontaneous protein ligation as a model reaction, we examined how the physicochemical microenvironment within condensates modulates reaction kinetics. We systematically analyzed condensates formed by folded PRM–SH3 scaffolds and intrinsically disordered proteins (LAF, TAF, and FUS). We designed a proximity-sensitive client probe to assess excluded-volume-driven increases in effective reactant concentration. In parallel, we characterized condensate hydrophilicity and associated changes in water activity, identifying these properties as additional key kinetic determinants. Together, our findings elucidate how effective concentration and hydrophilicity jointly regulate biochemical reactions within condensates.

articles_hidden.title: Training of human spatial skills: Brain activity as a window to the mind’s eye
articles_hidden.authors: Mary Hegarty

articles_hidden.title: Activation of ROPGEFs by a malectin-like receptor kinase is involved in tip growth regulation in Physcomitrium patens
articles_hidden.authors: Ruohan Lyu, Jingtong Ruan, Ying Chen, Haoyu Tian, Peishan Yi
articles_hidden.abstract: Rho-type GTPases of plants (ROPs) play essential roles in polarized cell growth, cell division, and organogenesis. Their activation depends on two types of guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs): the plant-specific PRONE-domain-containing ROPGEFs and DOCK-type SPKGEFs. While ROPGEFs have been proposed to be autoinhibited in pollen and activated by receptor-like kinases (RLKs), the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Using the moss Physcomitrium patens , we show that moss ROPGEF4 and ROPGEF6 exhibit low intrinsic GEF activity and are not autoinhibited by non-PRONE regions, whereas the catalytic domain of SPK1 and SPK6 is highly active. Through a candidate screen, we identified MLRK1, a malectin-like receptor kinase, as a ROPGEF-interacting protein. MLRK1 directly phosphorylates ROPGEF4 and ROPGEF6 and stimulates their GEF activities in vitro. These effects are attenuated by substituting key phosphosites (Ser231 in ROPGEF4 and Ser524/Thr526 in ROPGEF6) with nonphosphorylatable residues. Structural modeling, pull-down assays, and functional analyses indicate that phosphorylation enhances ROPGEF-ROP interactions and promotes the membrane localization of ROPGEF4/6. Furthermore, ROPGEFs are not essential for polarized cell growth on their own but act redundantly with SPK2. At the apical membrane, ROPGEFs appear to activate ROPs, reduce their diffusion, promote actin filament assembly and vesicle secretion, and ultimately facilitate cell expansion and growth. Collectively, our findings provide functional evidence that RLK-ROPGEF-ROP signaling module has emerged in early land plants and is involved in cell growth regulation.

articles_hidden.title: ACSS2 modulates endothelial glycolysis in angiogenesis
articles_hidden.authors: Yunyun Wang, Qingqiao Zha, Rong-Mo Zhang, Hong Chen, He Cai, Jingyi Xiang, Yaohui Kou, Cong Qiu, Lei Zhang, Michael Simons, Luyang Yu, Xiaolong Zhu
articles_hidden.abstract: Endothelial cells (ECs) sustain high glycolytic flux and display remarkable metabolic plasticity. Although molecular pathways regulating endothelial glycolysis are well characterized, metabolic mechanisms underlying hypoxia-induced glycolytic activation during angiogenesis remain poorly understood. Here, we show that acetyl-CoA synthetase 2 (ACSS2) serves as a critical metabolic modulator, coupling acetate utilization with glycolytic flux to control EC function and angiogenesis. The high level of ACSS2-mediated acetate-to-acetyl-CoA conversion in angiogenic front ECs sustains acetyl-CoA levels, which are essential for EC proliferation and retinal vascularization. Conversely, endothelial-specific Acss2 deletion disrupts pathological angiogenesis and normalizes tumor vasculature. Mechanistically, ACSS2 maintains hypoxia-inducible factor 1α transcriptional activity and stabilizes glucose transporter 1, thereby preserving glycolysis. Pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 4 knockdown rescues metabolic and functional defects in ACSS2-deficient ECs, revealing the vital role of acetyl-CoA homeostasis in modulating hypoxic endothelial metabolism. Taken together, these data establish ACSS2 as a pivotal regulator of vascular development and suggest that targeting acetate metabolism may be an effective way to modulate pathological angiogenesis.

articles_hidden.title: Domain-encoded DNA barcodes for combinatorial multiplexed protein imaging via stepwise displacement
articles_hidden.authors: Hang Xiao, Wei Cui, Yu Chen, Zongkang Guo, Wen Cheng, Qiuping Guo, Xiaohai Yang, Kemin Wang, Jin Huang
articles_hidden.abstract: Multiplexed protein imaging via DNA barcoding faces a fundamental scaling constraint: Each target requires a distinct DNA identity, making barcode capacity grow only linearly with the number of validated sequences. Combinatorial encoding in RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization achieves exponential scaling by distributing shared readout sequences across dozens of probes per transcript, but antibody-based protein labeling lacks this multiprobe architecture. Here, we report domain-encoded DNA barcodes (DEDBs), which embed combinatorial identity within the internal domain organization of a single-stranded DNA scaffold. Three orthogonal encoding units arranged across three encoding domains define a theoretical design space of 27 barcodes. Sequence reuse does not compromise readout specificity: Each read strand spans two adjacent domains, so a mismatched read strand inevitably contains a continuous stretch of noncomplementary bases and forms a thermodynamically disfavored intermediate that is subsequently displaced by the perfectly matched strand. We term this self-correcting behavior thermodynamic proofreading, and a three-process kinetic model shows that specificity arises not from initial binding discrimination but from cognate-driven correction at the product level. Coupled with signal-amplified antibody labeling, DEDBs enable quantitatively decoded nine-target intracellular protein imaging in fixed cells. The same barcode library supports Polychrome trajectory decoding for combinatorial identification and Monochrome cycle-resolved visualization for direct single-target inspection through reconfiguration of read-strand labeling. By generating combinatorial identities through the positional arrangement of reusable sequences within a single DNA strand, DEDBs reframe DNA barcode design from sequence enumeration to positional encoding.

articles_hidden.title: Durable CD8-mediated remission after brief anti-HIV-1 antibody treatment requires FcγR engagement
articles_hidden.authors: Stylianos Bournazos, Yoshiaki Nishimura, Barbara Ann C. Grace, Emily G. Niejadlik, Daniel C. Rogan, Tyler Meeks, Jonathan D. Webber, Paulina A. Przygonska, Hadrien Lehman, Veronica E. Minster, Eric Jesteadt, Reza Sadjadpour, Mark Connors, Malcolm A. Martin, Jeffrey V. Ravetch
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite highly efficacious antiretroviral therapy (ART), durable ART-free remission remains a central objective of HIV-1 cure strategies. The randomized, placebo-controlled RIO trial recently demonstrated that long-acting broadly neutralizing anti-HIV-1 antibodies (bNAbs) can sustain prolonged virologic control after ART interruption, including control that persisted beyond the period of therapeutically relevant antibody concentrations, providing clinical evidence consistent with host-mediated suppression. However, the mechanisms underlying these “vaccinal” effects remain unresolved. Here, we establish Fcγ receptor (FcγR) engagement as an essential driver of multiyear remission after bNAb therapy in simian-human immunodeficiency virus (SHIV)-infected macaques. Brief therapy during acute infection with Fc domain variants of the bNAb 3BNC117, matched for antigen binding, neutralizing activity, and pharmacokinetics but differing in FcγR engagement, produced comparable early virologic control yet profoundly divergent long-term outcomes. Sustained CD8 T cell–dependent suppression lasting nearly 300 wk developed in every evaluable animal receiving the FcγR-engaging variant but arose in only one of eight recipients of the FcγR-null variant. FcγR-driven immunomodulation imprinted a CD8 T cell response characterized by enhanced antigen-specific effector function, early clonal focusing with sustained clonotype persistence, and distinct cellular-state transcriptional signatures. Our findings identify the Fc–FcγR axis as a critical determinant of the reliable induction of durable remission and provide a mechanistic framework for developing Fc-engineered bNAbs designed to enhance vaccinal immunity and advance antibody-based strategies with the potential to achieve functional cure.

articles_hidden.title: Pollen tubes beat the heat
articles_hidden.authors: Sharon A. Kessler

articles_hidden.title: Cryo-EM provides insight into how the Staphylococcus aureus IsdH receptor removes hemin from the hemoglobin:haptoglobin complex
articles_hidden.authors: Jess Soule, Brendan J. Mahoney, Andrew K. Goring, Joseph A. Loo, Jose A. Rodriguez, Robert T. Clubb
articles_hidden.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus extracts hemin from human hemoglobin (Hb) to overcome host-imposed iron limitation. How it recovers Hb-bound hemin from the hemoglobin:haptoglobin (Hb:Hp) complex, the major circulating form of Hb outside red blood cells, remains unclear. Here, we use cryo-electron microscopy, biophysical measurements, and solution kinetics to define how the S. aureus IsdH surface receptor extracts hemin from Hb:Hp. A 3.1 Å cryo-EM structure of Hb:Hp bound by full-length IsdH reveals that its N-terminal NEAT domain (N1) anchors it to αHb, whereas its downstream N2N3 extraction unit engages βHb to remove its hemin. The receptor engages Hb:Hp differently than isolated Hb, because N-linked glycans on haptoglobin bias the extraction unit toward βHb, sterically occluding its access to αHb while still permitting engagement by N1. Kinetic assays show that IsdH actively accelerates hemin release from Hb:Hp. Three-dimensional variability analysis indicates that this likely occurs via a dynamic interface in which receptor motions reposition the extraction unit relative to βHb, collectively supporting a model in which IsdH transiently perturbs the F-helix to promote hemin extraction. Alignment of that model with a previously determined CD163:Hb:Hp structure shows how IsdH may disrupt Hb:Hp recognition by macrophage and monocyte CD163 receptors, helping to explain how it may hinder clearance of Hb:Hp from circulation. In aggregate, these results help define the structural basis for hemin extraction from Hb:Hp and how IsdH may subvert receptor-mediated clearance of the Hb:Hp complex.

articles_hidden.title: Structural insights into inhibition and activation mechanisms of plant calcium-dependent protein kinases
articles_hidden.authors: Shan-Yue Zhao, Hui-Fang Hu, Zhipu Luo, Jing Lv, Ying-Nan Liu, Jia-Wei Wu, Zhi-Xin Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) comprise the major group of Ca 2+ -regulated kinases in plants and protists. These enzymes comprise an N-terminal kinase domain and a C-terminal Ca 2+ -dependent activation domain (CAD). We solved the crystal structures of autoinhibited and activated forms of a plant CDPK, Arabidopsis CPK3. In the autoinhibited form, the CAD resembles a “dumbbell-like” calmodulin protein with a long helix in the N terminus that inhibits the kinase domain in a pseudo-substrate manner. Upon Ca 2+ binding to the four EF-hands, CAD undergoes a dramatic conformational change with a rotation around the kinase domain, thus exposing its active site for substrate recognition. Our structural and biochemical studies reveal that most plant CDPKs may involve distinct mechanisms of activation compared with CDPKs from the apicomplexan parasites.

articles_hidden.title: Localization mechanisms and function of postsynaptic K v 7 (KCNQ) channels and their reduction in KCNQ2 epileptic encephalopathy
articles_hidden.authors: Sahil Malpotra, Hongyu Zhao, Gregory C. Tracy, Angelina R. Wilton, Gloria W. Lau, Jiaren Zhang, Kyoeun Keum, Logan Silzer, Paul R. Selvin, Anastasios V. Tzingounis, Hee Jung Chung
articles_hidden.abstract: K v 7 channels composed of K v 7.2 and K v 7.3 subunits are enriched in neuronal axons where their hyperpolarizing potassium current suppresses repetitive and burst firing of action potentials. Mutations in their genes, KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 , cause neonatal epilepsy, underscoring their critical role in regulating neuronal excitability. In this study, we provide evidence that K v 7 channels are present at and near the postsynaptic density within dendritic spines of hippocampal neurons, where their current decreases calcium influx through NMDA receptors. This spine localization is promoted by heteromerization of K v 7.2 and K v 7.3 and their binding to AnkyrinG-190, which is the only AnkyrinG isoform present in dendritic spines. Lastly, spine localization of K v 7 channels and their ability to suppress NMDA receptor activity are markedly reduced by select variants of KCNQ2 that cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). These findings reveal a subcellular population of K v 7 channels that can dampen excitatory synaptic transmission and implicate their dysregulation in KCNQ2 -associated DEE.

articles_hidden.title: Supercritical snapping and controlled launching via dual-latch gels
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaona M. Xu, Anyang Wang, Nolan A. Miller, Nianqiang Wu, Gregory M. Grason, Alfred J. Crosby
articles_hidden.abstract: Natural organisms have evolved integrated Latch-Mediated Spring Actuation systems (LaMSA) that consist of multiple latches and springs to enhance power output and adapt to diverse environmental conditions. Similar designs are appealing yet largely unexplored in engineered materials due to the complexity of integrating multiple components into a single material platform. Here, we report a dual-latch magneto-elastic shell device capable of selectively activating the latches to regulate snapping pathways and energy output based on specific actuation requirements. Differential deswelling across the thickness acts as the “motor” to load the elastic energy into the shell, which is then released via the snap-through instability once the loading reaches the critical threshold, constituting an intrinsic mechanical latch. Activation of the external magnetic latch delays snapping onset beyond the threshold of the intrinsic latch, leading to a power-amplified supercritical snap-through instability as well as a bifurcation instability. The combined function of both latches allows for flexible control over energy storage and release. Additionally, this integrated LaMSA system possesses an untethered anchoring mechanism, enabling the device to launch in arbitrary directions from the substrate, driven by the energy released during snapping. We envision that the design principles of dual-latch LaMSA systems will create opportunities for power-dense actuation in engineered materials and robotic devices.

articles_hidden.title: Lactate-rich tumor employs the KAT5–HIF1α axis to modulate the activity of the hypoxia pathway and facilitates tumor progression
articles_hidden.authors: Zhaoxiang Wang, Zhengyan Liang, Yingzhi Chen, Xia Kong, Zhiguo Wang, Panpan Zhu, Hewen Ye, Jiao Yuan, Jiayue Wen, Weixian Zhou, Ying Xue, Yongkang Zou, Zhiwei He, Junzhi Zhou
articles_hidden.abstract: Substantial evidence shows that hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF1α) up-regulates glycolytic enzymes and promotes lactate production, which contributes to “Warburg Effect.” Nevertheless, the impact of lactate or lactylation modification on hypoxia signaling pathways within the tumor microenvironment remains largely unclear. Here, we report that lactate can induce the upregulation of hypoxia pathway activity in a HIF1α-dependent manner. We identified that KAT5 as a lysine lactyltransferase of HIF1α and the “writer” responsible for lactylation at HIF1α K389, K460, K674, and K682, and HDAC2 as a HIF1α de-lactylase. The lactylation-deficient mutant of HIF1α (HIF1α 4KR ) reduced HIF1α stability, along with down-regulating hypoxia-mediated angiogenesis, metastasis, apoptosis, and glycolysis. Mechanistically, the HIF1α 4KR mutant enhances the binding of HIF1α to von Hippel-Lindau tumor suppressor protein (VHL), facilitating its degradation. MG149, a KAT5 inhibitor, can enhance the efficacy of anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)-based combination immunotherapy in a murine model by suppressing hypoxia pathway activity in tumor cells and potentiating the cytotoxic function of CD8 + T cells. Clinically, lactylated HIF1α and KAT5 are up-regulated in breast cancer tissues compared with adjacent tissues. Notably, elevated levels of HIF1α lactylation and KAT5 expression were observed in resistant cancer specimens from triple-negative breast cancer patients who had undergone neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. Our results indicate that the tumor lactate microenvironment promotes the formation of the tumor hypoxic microenvironment by hijacking and lactylating HIF1α, and the KAT5–HIF1α Kla axis presents a promising therapeutic target for hypoxic tumors.

articles_hidden.title: Coevolving gene networks underlying a phenotypic syndrome revealed via integrating comparative genomic and microevolutionary analyses
articles_hidden.authors: Saurav Baral, Sridhar Halali, Mats Ittonen, Klaus Fischer, Karl Gotthard, Christopher W. Wheat
articles_hidden.abstract: Complex adaptive traits often comprise interacting, coevolving phenotypes that together for a syndrome that is shaped by multiple genetic loci. While using intraspecific variation is an established approach for investigating syndromes, such polymorphism typically captures only a subset of syndrome traits. Diapause, an alternative developmental pathway that evolved independently in many species to synchronize life cycles with resource availability, exemplifies this challenge. While subsets of this essential phenotype have long been studied at a single species level, the genomic basis of the full diapause syndrome remains poorly understood. This paucity of insights has fueled a long-standing debate about how life cycle synchronization evolves and whether convergent phenotypes employ shared mechanisms. Using a comparative genomic analysis spanning diverse diapause transitions in butterflies, we identified a large network of coevolving genes unique to diapausing species. The network is composed of functional modules spanning circadian regulation, metabolism, and cell cycle control. We tested whether this macroevolutionary scale network predicts microevolutionary dynamics, hypothesizing that this network is the polygenic architecture underlying the diapause syndrome. Analyses revealed that allelic variation in the diapause network is significantly enriched in signatures of local adaptation across latitudes, but only in diapausing species. Thus, we empirically show that diapause evolves through modular, coevolving gene networks, components of which impact intraspecific variation in diapause. Using this integrative perspective on a complex phenotype opens a horizon of inquiry for understanding seasonal adaptation across evolutionary scales, while demonstrating the power of integrating comparative genomics with microevolutionary dynamics to dissect complex phenotypic syndromes.

articles_hidden.title: Authentic structure of the CCHFV RNA–nucleoprotein complex at near-atomic resolution
articles_hidden.authors: Zidan Song, Nan Zhang, Fan Wu, Wentao Ni, Yixiao Liu, Dongdong Sun, Bowen Zhang, Jingwu Jian, Wenli Zhao, Xi Wang, Lulu Wang, Hang Shang, Yuhui Wang, Wenming Wang, Zhiyong Lou, Yajie Liu, Zhihong Hu, Zihe Rao, Bo Huang, Yucen Huang, Wei Zheng, Manli Wang, Yu Guo
articles_hidden.abstract: Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) poses a major public health threat without approved vaccines or antivirals. Its ribonucleoprotein (RNP) is essential for replication, but its native architecture and RNA packaging remain elusive. Here, we combine AI-based structural prediction with cryo–electron microscopy to resolve the native structure of the CCHFV RNP purified from CCHFV-infected cells. We report a 3.87 Å structure of a single-turn RNP, and local refinement yielded a 3.55 Å structure of two adjacent NP protomers with continuous RNA. This represents the highest-resolution authentic RNP structure reported among segmented negative-strand RNA viruses (sNSVs), and provides the structural basis for CCHFV RNP assembly. Together with mutational analyses, these findings define the molecular basis of RNA encapsidation and NP oligomerization in the native CCHFV RNP. Our findings provide a hybrid structural framework integrating AI and experimental approaches for understanding genome organization in sNSVs and offer a foundation for future antiviral development.

articles_hidden.title: Distinct nanoscale architectures of GABAergic inhibitory synapses predict diverse synaptic output
articles_hidden.authors: Amber R. Stewart, Sara E. Gookin, Joshua D. Garcia, Katlin H. Zent, Kevin C. Crosby, Katharine R. Smith
articles_hidden.abstract: GABAergic synaptic inhibition is heterogenous across neuronal compartments, and plays a critical role in shaping local, cellular, and circuit excitability. In pyramidal neurons, inhibition is mediated by GABA A receptors (GABA A Rs) clustered at the inhibitory postsynaptic domain (iPSD). Synaptic strength depends not only on the number of GABA A Rs within the iPSD, but also on their precise nanoscale organization into discrete subsynaptic domains (SSDs). These SSDs often align with presynaptic GABA release sites to form nanocolumn structures that enhance synaptic efficacy. While nanocolumn organization is increasingly recognized as a key determinant of synaptic function, most studies of GABAergic synapses have focused on archetypal dendritic synapses, which control the plasticity and integration of excitatory inputs. Nonetheless, it remains unclear whether somatic synapses—which deliver robust inhibition to suppress neuronal output—share a similar nanoarchitecture. Here, we used complementary superresolution imaging approaches to directly compare inhibitory synapses in somatic and dendritic compartments. We found that somatic synapses are larger and exhibit greater structural diversity and nanoscale complexity than dendritic synapses. Dendritic synapses display relatively compact architectures with GABA A R SSDs frequently arranged into nanocolumns. In contrast, somatic synapses show a broader range of organizations, including aligned nanocolumns as well as more disorganized configurations with misaligned release sites or receptor SSDs, arrangements that likely exhibit input-specificity. Computational modeling revealed that these structural differences produce distinct functional outcomes, including increased inhibitory postsynaptic current amplitude and altered kinetics at somatic synapses. Together, our findings demonstrate that nanoscale organization differentially shapes inhibitory strength and signaling properties across neuronal compartments.

articles_hidden.title: Localized end-on heating for hot spot ignition in precompressed isochoric plasmas
articles_hidden.authors: Bofang Jiang, Han Xu, Zekun Xu, Bo Zeng, Fuyuan Wu, Ge Zhou, Xiaohu Yang, Qi Zhang, Huanyu Song, Ke Fang, Yihang Zhang, Xiaohui Yuan, Zhe Zhang, Dawei Yuan, Chenglong Zhang, ChuanQi Shi, Zhijie Qiu, Weimin Wang, Xuechun Li, Yutong Li, Jingquan Liu, Jian Zheng, Jianqiang Zhu, Jie Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: In fast ignition inertial confinement fusion, a “heating cone” is employed to shorten the transport distance of the relativistic electron beam (REB) to the high-density plasma core, thereby mitigating energy losses at the plasma edge.
